items.title: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month
items.description: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Oct 29, 2026 Highlights In 2026Q3, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County registered at $2,554,—down $96, or 3.6%, from a year earlier. The median asking rent for 0-2 bedrooms in L.A. County was $2,239, reflecting a decline of $88 (-3.8%) from the previous year. Meanwhile, rent for 3+ bedroom units dropped by $70 (-1.9%) compared to 2025Q3, standing at $3,571. For renters in L.A. County : Buying costs far more than renting. In 2026Q3, a median-priced home cost $4,716 more a month than renting one, nearly 185% higher, even though the monthly buying cost fell about 2% as home prices dropped. Mortgage rates above 7% could erase that relief. At 7%, the same home would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the savings from lower prices In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for all rental properties listed on Realtor.com in Los Angeles County was $2,554, a decline of $96, or 3.6%, compared with a year ago. While the county experienced a temporary dip in rents during the pandemic, asking rents quickly rebounded to pre-pandemic levels and peaked in the summer of 2022. Since then, a surge in new multifamily construction has put sustained downward pressure on rent. In the most recent quarter, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County was $340, or 11.7%, below its 2022 peak. In addition, Los Angeles County renters are overwhelmingly local. In the third quarter of 2026, more than half (61.3%) of online traffic to L.A. County rental listings originated from within the county, with an additional 15.5% coming from elsewhere in California. Out-of-state renters accounted for 19.8% of traffic, while international traffic represented 3.4%. Breaking down by bedroom type, the median asking rent for 0-2 bedroom units in Los Angeles County was $2,239 in 2026Q3, a decline of $88 or 3.8%, from a year ago. Larger units with three or more bedrooms saw a comparatively modest softening, with a median asking rent of $3,571 — down $70, or 1.9%, year-over-year. The steeper rent decline among smaller units suggests renters in that segment are experiencing greater pricing relief. The surge in ADUs across Los Angeles County may partially explain this trend. As those permitted units complete construction — typically requiring 6 to 18 months from permit to occupancy — a growing wave of new small rental units has been entering the market, adding downward price pressure concentrated in the smaller unit segment. Consistent with the broader L.A. County trend, rents in the City of Los Angeles have been on a downward trajectory since peaking in the summer of 2022. While the current median remains $158, or 5.5%, above pre-pandemic levels, renters today are saving $363 per month, or 11.8%, compared to the 2022 peak, translating to $4,356 in annual savings. Nevertheless, in order to afford a typical home in the city of Los Angeles, a minimum annual income of $108,320 is required— 22.1% higher than the city's estimated median household income of $88,730 1 High mortgage rates squeeze renters hoping to buy Renters may be catching a break, but for most renters who want to become homeowners in L.A. County, homeownership remains out of reach. On top of that, with mortgage rates now above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push homeownership even further out of reach for renters who want to buy. In 2026Q3, buying a typical home in L.A. County costs $4,716 more per month than renting one. Buying got slightly cheaper over the past year because home prices fell, even as mortgage rates rose. The median listing price dropped 3.2% to $970,000 over the past year, which more than offset a small increase in the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, from 6.57% to 6.68%. As a result, the estimated monthly cost of buying a median-priced home fell about 2.1%, or $159, from a year earlier, to $7,270. But that relief may not last. Rates surpassed 7% in late-September and remain well- above this mark. At 7%, the same home price would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the monthly payment savings from lower prices. Methodology To determine the monthly cost of buying a home, we find the median listing price for homes in Los Angeles County. As first-time homebuyers plan lower down payments, we assume a 10% down payment and use the 30-year fixed mortgage rate during the quarter to calculate a monthly mortgage payment. We also include the HOA fees, taxes, and homeowners insurance as part of the costs. L.A. rental data as of 2026Q3 for all units advertised for rent on Realtor.com®. Rental units include apartments as well as private rentals (condos, townhomes, single-family homes). We use rental sources that reliably report data each month within L.A. county. To calculate the median asking rent for each quarter, we first obtain the median asking rent for each month within that quarter and then take the average of the three months. items.title: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Oct. 24, 2026)
items.description: Weekly Housing Trends: U.S. Market Update (Week Ending Oct. 24, 2026) By Jiayi Xu Oct 29, 2026 Welcome to this weekly housing trends update, where we bring you the latest snapshot of inventory trends, listing activity, and buyer-seller dynamics across the U.S. housing market. In addition to our monthly housing trends reports , which offer deeper insights into long-term patterns, we publish these weekly updates to provide more timely views into market changes. This effort began in response to rapid shifts in the economy and housing landscape. You can count on a new Weekly Housing Trends update, fresh weekly data each Thursday, and a weekly video from our economists to help you stay informed. What this week’s data shows This week’s housing data reflects a market increasingly weighed down by renewed rate pressure. With mortgage rates topping 7%, hesitation is spreading across both sides of the market — buyers are pulling back, leaving homes to sit longer and unsold listings to accumulate, while sellers grow equally reluctant to list. Yet there are glimmers of hope: mortgage rates have eased from their recent peak , offering modest relief to budget sensitive buyers— though a more meaningful drop would be needed to meaningfully shift the landscape. On the seller side, the share of price cuts has hit a four-year high and the share of listings pulled from the market remains in line with a year ago — both signs that sellers, though cautious, are still committed to closing deals. For buyers, the key is preparation: rate-proofing their budget now and ensuring they are financially positioned to move when the right opportunity arises. Active inventory climbed 8.0% year-over-year The number of homes for sale rose 8.0% compared to a year ago, the highest weekly growth rate since late January. Inventory has been building momentum throughout the fall, rising from roughly 4% year-over-year growth in late August to 8% now. The pickup is not being driven by a flood of new sellers. Instead, the slowdown in buyer activity is allowing unsold listings to accumulate, pushing the overall count higher. Year-to-date, active inventory i s up 4.8%. Homes spent 1 day longer on the market compared to a year ago Median days on market came in at 64 days, with homes selling one day slower than the same time last year — snapping a streak of faster or matching pace that had held since late May. As mortgage rates top 7%, more buyers are retreating to the sidelines, and the shift could be an early signal of market slowdown. Year-to-date, time on market remains 2 days behind last year’s pace, as the sluggish start to 2025 continues to weigh on the cumulative figure. New listings, a measure of sellers putting homes up for sale, fell 1.5% year-over-year New listing activity continues to slow down, drop 1.5% year over year. Sellers are discouraged because buyers are discouraged. The prices the market will bear are less appealing to sellers than they were when mortgage rates were lower, and the difference between current rates and the rates many would-be sellers are sitting on in their has grown, making relocating a less attractive proposition. The stronger new listing activity earlier in the year has the year-to-date change at -0.3%. The median listing price fell 1.4% year-over-year The median listing price dropped to $414,000, down 1.4% from the same week last year. Listing prices have now been negative on a year-over-year basis for 41 consecutive weeks. The median price per square foot also declined, falling 1.3% year over year. Mortgage rates have buyers in an affordability crunch that has diminished their willingness to pay, and the median price in the market is slowly responding. Year-to-date, median listing prices sit 1.9% below 2025 levels.

items.title: Mortgage Rates Fall 8 Basis Points for the Second Week in a Row
items.description: Mortgage Rates Fall 8 Basis Points for the Second Week in a Row By Joel Berner Oct 29, 2026 What happened to mortgage rates this week? The Freddie Mac 30-year mortgage rate dropped 8 basis points this week, from 7.32% to 7.24%, in conjunction with the 10-year Treasury yield, which averaged about 5.02% in the past week compared to 5.13% the week prior. The retreat in the Treasury yield was spurred on by volatility in the stock market, leading investors to seek safety in government debt. It could be argued that weak housing market data, namely softer home construction activity , record-low pending sales , and declining new home sales , are creating a feedback loop as well. A struggling housing market can be a sign of weaker economic growth to come, which lowers the returns investors demand on their bond purchases. In turn, this allows mortgage rates to fall and hopefully alleviate some of the negative effects being experienced by the housing market. The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee met yesterday and left the target interest rate unchanged , but two members dissented in favor of a 25 bps hike. Prediction markets already favored a hike in December, but that likelihood grew higher after the release. Expectations of further Fed tightening are widespread, but the upcoming data releases on inflation and employment before December 9th will give stronger indication of whether upward pressure on mortgage rates is in store. The Fed appears laser-focused on the price level, and another month of core inflation coming in above their target of 2% would justify those rate hike expectations. What does this mean for the housing market? This week’s retreat in mortgage rates is certainly welcome news to anyone involved with the housing market, but it comes during a period in the year where home sales activity is usually more muted anyway. The best time of year to buy a home has passed for most markets in the country, and the winter slowdown is upcoming, so the rate relief this week may not have much of an impact on the market. Both buyers and sellers are hoping that the downward trajectory of the last two weeks is a sign of things to come, and that the great housing market unlocking becomes a reality in 2027.

DOWNLOAD THE Q3 2026 REPORT Key Takeaways Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 msf underway. Vacancy increased 10 bps QOQ to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 psf in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. Supply Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 million square feet (msf) underway. Construction commenced on nearly 63,000 square feet (sf) of new retail space during the quarter. Meanwhile, deliveries totaled 78,000 sf, bringing year-to-date (YTD) deliveries to 158,000 sf. This represented a 64.6% year-over-year (YOY) decrease from the 447,000 sf delivered during the same period in 2025. Vacancy increased 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Despite the slight increase, Miami-Dade County’s retail market continued to demonstrate tight conditions, with vacancy remaining the lowest among Florida markets, below Fort Lauderdale at 4.2%, Orlando at 3.9% and Tampa at 3.8%. Demand Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. The market recorded negative 81,000 sf of net absorption during the quarter, bringing the YTD total to negative 129,000 sf. Although occupancy losses have persisted in six of the past seven quarters, quarterly performance improved considerably from negative 230,000 sf in the third quarter of 2025. At the submarket level, Kendall and Miami Airport led occupancy gains, recording 97,000 sf and nearly 51,000 sf of positive absorption, respectively. These gains were offset by losses in Coral Gables (negative 41,000 sf) and Northeast Dade (negative 35,000 sf). By property type, malls posted the strongest performance, with occupancy gains of just under 12,000 sf, while general retail recorded the largest decline at negative 62,000 sf. Overall, leasing activity and occupancy trends remained mixed across the county, with gains in select submarkets and property types offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Looking ahead, the construction pipeline may provide additional opportunities for retailers as new space enters the market, although future occupancy gains will depend on demand keeping pace with new supply. Pricing Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 per square foot (psf) in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Among the county’s retail submarkets, Miami Beach commanded the highest average asking rent at $97.85 psf, while Miami recorded the lowest at $31.92 psf. Compared YOY, average asking rents increased in 16 submarkets and declined in three. Outlying Miami-Dade County recorded the largest YOY increase, with rents rising 4.1% from $40.97 psf to $42.65 psf. In contrast, Brickell asking rents declined 2.4% YOY to $84.96 psf. Retail Sales Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. This brought YTD transaction volume to $1.2 billion across 2.0 msf. YTD transaction volume declined 25.5% YOY and was 6.6% below the five-year average. Miami Airport led all submarkets with $265.8 million in sales. Notable transactions included the $72.0 million sale of Airpark Plaza, located at 5715 NW Seventh Street in the Miami Airport submarket. By property type, strip malls recorded the highest average sale price at $815 psf during the quarter. Pricing remained elevated, with Miami averaging $450 psf, well above the U.S. average of $246 psf, underscoring the market’s continued premium positioning. Miami-Dade County’s retail capitalization rates ranged from 4.9% to 7.2%, averaging 5.8%. This was below the national average of 7.4%, indicating that local retail properties continued to trade at lower yields than the national average. items.title: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter
items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent. items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 10/29/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.24% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.60% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline Further to 7.24% The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.24% as of October 29, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.32%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.17%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.60%, down from last week when it averaged 6.68%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). Changes in Information Shared In 1984 , the 1-year ARM was added to the survey. In 1991 , the 15-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was added. In January 2005 , a 5/1 hybrid ARM series was added. In January 2016 , the 1-year ARM was discontinued. In November 2022 , adjustable rates and fees/points were discontinued. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . items.title: PCE Inflation Accelerated in September
items.description: PCE Inflation Accelerated in September October 29, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge accelerated in September after holding at 3.0% for three consecutive months, complicating the Fed's path to its 2% target. Consumer spending continued to be pushed up by elevated energy prices rather than income growth, driving the personal saving rate to the lowest level in nearly four years. The headline Personal Consumption Expenditure (PCE) Price Index increased 3.6% in September from a year ago, the fastest pace since May, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis . The “core” PCE price index, which excludes food and energy, rose 3.1% over the past twelve months, following a 3.0% increase last month. Core PCE has remained at or above 3.0% since the start of the Iran conflict, suggesting inflation pressure persists even excluding volatile energy prices. Consumer spending rose 0.5% in September, while real spending, adjusted to remove inflation, remained unchanged. Meanwhile, personal income rose 0.2% in September. This growth was led by increases in compensation and government social benefits. Real disposable income—income adjusted for taxes and inflation—fell 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, personal income was 4.1% higher, and real (inflation-adjusted) disposable income was up 1.0%. With spending growth outpacing income growth, the personal saving rate fell to 3.8% in September, the lowest level since November 2022. items.title: U.S. Home-Sale Prices Just Fell for the First Time in 3 Years
items.description: U.S. Home-Sale Prices Just Fell for the First Time in 3 Years Published on October 29th, 2026 by Dana Anderson The median monthly mortgage payment is still sitting at its second-highest level on record, spooking would-be buyers. What to know about the U.S. housing market for the four weeks ending October 25: The median U.S. home-sale price has fallen for the first time in more than three years . The median home-sale price was $389,601, down 0.1% year over year. That marks the second straight week in which prices ticked down–it follows a 0.2% decline last week–after three straight years of increases. Homebuying demand fell to a new low. Pending home sales declined 1.8% from a week earlier to the lowest level in records dating back to 2021. For the third week in a row, pending sales declined in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metro areas. The typical homebuyer’s monthly payment hit its second-highest level on record. The median mortgage payment was $2,786, up 10.7% year over year to the highest level in our record except the prior week. The weekly average mortgage rate is 7.32% , down from 7.4% a week earlier but still near a three-year high. Would-be sellers pulled back. New listings declined 0.6% from a week earlier to their lowest level since the start of the year as homeowners react to slow homebuying demand. Total supply is creeping up. The total number of homes for sale ticked up 0.3% from a week earlier. Even though new listings are falling, pending sales are falling more, keeping the pool of inventory partly filled. There are hundreds of thousands more home sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they’ve had in over a decade. items.title: RealTrends Verified brokerage Howard Hanna enters Alabama with ARC, Capstone deal
items.description: Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is entering Alabama through a partnership with ARC Realty and Capstone Realty , adding 875 agents across 12 offices in Birmingham, Montgomery and Huntsville. ARC and Capstone operate as Alabama’s largest real estate brokerage and will continue to do business under their existing brands while joining Howard Hanna’s national network, according to an announcement on Wednesday. The move gives Pittsburgh-based Howard Hanna , a RealTrends Verified brokerage, a foothold in one of the Southeast’s faster-growing housing markets while extending its footprint to 19 states. The family-owned brokerage now spans more than 500 offices with about 15,000 sales associates and staff. Howard Hanna’s partnership with ARC and Capstone comes a little over three months after the firm announced a similar partnership with the Maine-based Portside Real Estate Group , a RealTrends Verified brokerage . “This is very similar to the partnership with Portside,” Hoby Hanna, the CEO of Howard Hanna, told HousingWire . “A lot of the transactions we’ve been doing lately have been us acquiring a majority interest in the company and allowing local leadership to stay in and run the market as a partner.” Hanna, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said ARC Realty and Capstone Realty will retain local leadership and existing office structures while gaining access to Howard Hanna’s technology stack, marketing platform, referral network and affiliated mortgage, title and insurance services. “We think leadership is so valuable and important for everyone,” Hanna said. This means that both Beau Bevis , the CEO of ARC, and Darrin Hasley, the CEO of Capstone, are staying on board. “The local leaders are focused on growth, and we are bringing them the best products from Howard Hanna to add to the mix and just allowing them to really focus on the local marketplace and growing in their markets,” Hanna said. Partners in growth Hanna said this partnership strategy is one the company intends to employ moving forward as Howard Hanna looks to continue growing and expanding. “We have become a vehicle for owners of these types of independent brokerages to come to and say, ‘Maybe we can achieve more collectively and have greater strength to compete on innovation and to add mortgage title and insurance operations as new revenue sources,’” Hanna said, noting that the leaders of Portside, ARC and Capstone came to Howard Hanna looking for a partnership like this. “They had taken their businesses to a certain level, but they wanted to take it even greater. They felt that Howard Hanna could be a vehicle for them to do that by bringing new products, services, technology and innovation to the marketplace that they couldn't on their own in today's climate.” But Hanna noted that his firm won’t take just any company that comes knocking on their door, they must also share some of the same cultural values. Some of the central pillars to Howard Hanna’s culture, according to Hanna, are valuing leadership, financial stability and a focus on agent productivity and professional growth. “We don’t need to have the most agents in the business, but we want highly productive agents that want to be the best in the business,” Hanna said. “And it is expensive to have managers in an office, but having a level of management or a department of people who are committed to helping the agents grow and wanting to be leaders themselves is also important.” Hanna added he and his team have no interest in buying broken companies and trying to fix them, but instead want to enhance the companies and help them learn and grow. Looking ahead, Hanna said the firm will continue growing, focusing on opportunities West of the Mississippi River “with good, well run companies.” “I wouldn’t say there is any one specific place we are targeting, but with Portside and now with ARC and Capstone and the relationships of those leaders, we are talking to some firms in New England. I think we are expecting to see a bit more growth in the Southeast corridor between Alabama and where we are now in the Carolinas,” he said. But even as the firm continues growing, Hanna said they will only enter a partnership or an acquisition if it is the right fit for the overall company. “It is not like we have shareholders we have to answer to each quarter or a hedge fund telling us we have to do something this month to show growth,” Hanna said. “We can look for [partnerships] that are strategic.” Related More: Alabama Hoby Hanna Howard Hanna Real Estate Services

items.title: Freddie Mac's loan acquisitions top Fannie's as rates rise
items.description: Freddie Mac's loan acquisitions top Fannie's as rates rise By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 29, 2026, 3:27 p.m. EDT 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: See why Freddie Mac's new loan acquisitions moved ahead of Fannie Mae's in the third quarter. What's at Stake: Competition between Fannie and Freddie could make them more willing to open up the credit box for lenders who sell loans to them. A profitable Freddie Mac regained its lead over larger competitor Fannie Mae in single-family loan acquisitions during the third quarter as higher rates intensified competition between them. Freddie, which is the smaller of the two government-sponsored enterprises when it comes to its outstanding portfolio size, reported Thursday that it acquired $98 billion in home mortgages during the fiscal period. Fannie Mae , in comparison, purchased $88 billion in single-family loans. Processing Content These and other numbers in their recent earnings raises the question of what Freddie is doing to capture more loan acquisitions and whether it's opening up the credit box to do it. The latest underwriting indicators in earnings show Freddie's credit score and loan-to-value ratio tolerances are slightly higher, but the growth in credit reserves and some elevated delinquency measures at both GSEs suggests both will be cautious about the size of their credit boxes. "We are growing our financial strength, applying disciplined decision-making and risk management, and continuing to invest in the capabilities that can make the housing system work better," Freddie Mac Chief Financial Officer Jim Whitlinger said in the GSE's earnings call. What underwriting indicators show Whitlinger reported that Freddie's weighted average current loan-to-value ratio was 54% and the equivalent credit score was 755 in the company's third-quarter earnings call. Fannie's equivalent credit score number was 753 and its mark-to-market loan-to-value ratio was 51%. Current or mark-to-market LTVs on the outstanding portfolios account for property value changes and paydowns on loans over time. Weighted averages for original LTVs are generally higher and have averaged more around 78%, according to Fannie. The underwriting metrics for new acquisitions are a subset of the broader portfolio numbers. Whitlinger and others have indicated there may be more caution in that part of the market because slight increases in certain delinquency buckets have been driven by newer vintages. "The year-over-year increase was primarily driven by higher serious delinquency rates for loans originated during 2022 through 2024," Whitlinger said during the call. Both Fannie and Freddie have seen some delinquencies inch up in both their single- and multifamily book, calling for broader risk management. With risk growing, Freddie had to manage a larger-than anticipated shift from a $900 million benefit for credit losses to a $800 million reserve during the quarter, analysts at BTIG noted. Fannie also recorded a shift from a benefit for credit losses to a reserve in the period. All this suggests that for the time being, Freddie and Fannie are keeping an eye on credit, which may limit how much leeway in underwriting they want to use to compete. But they still want to offer some additional support to help consumers afford homes to the extent their delinquency rates and overall financials allow. While some types of arrears are rising, the single-family serious delinquency rate is still historically low at less than 1% at both GSEs. "Financial strength matters because of what it enables us to do," Whitlinger said. "It gives us greater capacity to provide liquidity throughout the economic cycle, support sustainable homeownership and help make housing finance more efficient and affordable." Examples include a lender option that both GSEs now offer to use the modernized VantageScore 4.0 credit metric for loan pricing, which some mortgage companies have said helped them get certain borrowers approved. This was used for 6% of the loans Fredddie bought in the third quarter, Whitlinger said. Other key financial metrics to watch The GSEs so far have shown that they are financially strong from a net income perspective and have sustained the long run of profitability that followed their 2008 move into conservatorship. So long as that financial strength persists, they might do more to expand some underwriting selectively with offsetting, more conservative adjustments in other areas in line with the trend seen in the condo market. Freddie reported that quarterly net income rose by around 17% on the year to $3.2 billion, and Fannie announced a day earlier that its strongest net revenues since 2023 drove an 8% increase during the same period to $4.2 billion. The smaller GSE's $3.2 billion in growth for the quarter also brought its total net worth to $81 billion, helping to close a regulatory capital gap that's also essential to their financial soundness and an eventual conservatorship exit. Fannie also reported improvement in this area. "Excluding buffers, our capital shortfall was $98 billion at the end of third quarter 2026, largely because the $73 billion of senior preferred stock does not qualify," Whitlinger said in a reminder that an exit would need to address this, a key point prominent GSE investors have emphasized. Adjusted for the SPS, this means capital is around $21 billion below its statutory minimum level, Keefe, Bruyette & Woods analysts noted in a report on Freddie's earnings. "FMCC's capital remains subordinate to the government's senior preferred shares and liquidation preference, so any privatization would have to include either forgiveness or conversion," the KBW analysts wrote. items.title: Office Recovery Moving Faster Than Expected, CoStar Finds
items.description: American office buildings are filling up faster than previously predicted, with a lack of new construction expected to drive vacancy lower through the next year. Unsplash/Khara Woods CoStar Group revised its office predictions through the end of next year to reflect rising demand for increasingly hard-to-find high-quality space. The ubiquitous online real estate marketplace now expects lower vacancy rates due in large part to an all-but-dead construction pipeline. “The latest forecast calls for a continuation of the slow-but-steady revival, with an ongoing supply-side adjustment offsetting historically weak office demand growth,” Phil Mobley , national director of office analytics at CoStar Group, said in a statement. CoStar projects absorption to be around 20M SF in 2026 and 9M SF in 2027, up from 13M SF and 5M SF, respectively, from its previous forecast released in August. Office vacancy is expected to end the year around 13.6%, just below the previous 13.7% forecast. High-quality properties will continue to drive pricing higher, with CoStar predicting asking rents will climb 2.5% in each of the next few quarters before rising closer to 3% annually. The upward revision to the rent forecast was more to do with a shift in inventory accounting than an expected boost in activity. “The upgraded projection for office rent growth has less to do with the overall reduction in supply caused by the removal of non-competitive space and more to do with the dramatic slowdown in new construction,” Mobley said. CoStar Group The office market has continued to rebound from pandemic-era lows, driven by demand from tech firms and the more general push from tenants into high-quality spaces. Leasing activity totaled 63.8M SF in the third quarter, up 4% from last year and on track to exceed a 2022 record, according to CBRE . Absorption was positive for the 10th consecutive quarter at just under 5M SF at the end of September, with the construction pipeline a paltry 1.5M SF, down 76% from the prior year. Rent growth is accelerating at its fastest pace since 2016, according to CBRE. Analysts at CoStar said the risks on either side of its forecast seemed roughly in balance in terms of probability, but with larger downside risks in terms of size. “Persistent inflation and higher interest rates could slow economic growth further and precipitate additional business cost-cutting even in an environment of continued economic expansion,” Mobley said. “Furthermore, the recent productivity gains evident in knowledge work could accelerate with further adoption of artificial intelligence , resulting in lower demand for some types of knowledge workers.” Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: CBRE , Colliers , CoStar , CoStar Group , Phil Mobley

items.title: National Inflation Averages Hide Local CRE Opportunities, Marcus & Millichap Says
items.description: National CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. National + Weekender | October 29, 2026 By: Amy Wolff Sorter National Inflation Averages Hide Local CRE Opportunities, Marcus & Millichap Says Higher-than-expected September inflation has been driving the CRE narrative of increased cost of capital, along with rising operating and construction expenses. The consumer price index rose 3.7% year-over-year in September, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, while the producer price index for final demand climbed 6.3% A recent Marcus & Millichap video said that the main inflation drivers have been energy prices, up 20.4% year-over- year , and transportation costs, up 7.8%. “But we have to remember that, while we have a national inflation rate, not all states or metros are facing the exact same cost increases,” Marcus & Millichap Senior Vice President John Chang said in the video. Metro-Level Differences Chang pointed out that, on a year-over-year basis, inflation was: 1.3% in Houston, TX 1.9% in Tampa, FL 2.5% in Phoenix, AZ On the other side of the spectrum, inflation stood at: 4.5% in New York, NY 4.7% in San Diego, CA 5.2% in Hawaii Diesel, a primary driver of inflation, shows the same pattern. Nationally, diesel averages about $6.30 per gallon. But the Chang said that diesel ran about $5.60 to $5.80 in North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Texas and Louisiana. Meanwhile, California reached about $8.50 per gallon, with prices in Washington, Oregon, Nevada and Hawaii ranging from about $6.75 to $7.30. "My point here is that national averages don't tell the whole story, and that carries over to commercial real estate," Chang said. Wide Ranges Within Property Types Chang acknowledged that broad trends, including elevated inflation, slowing job creation and rising interest rates, generate CRE headwinds that can impact cap rates. But the opposite is true when digging down to the metro, submarket and asset levels. For example, office cap rates differed, depending on the property: Apartment cap rates also showed a wide range: Chang said that many investors will push higher in the coming months, providing opportunities for investors. In addition, “motivated sellers are already reevaluating their pricing, creating unique investment opportunities," he added. Overall, the national economic and investment headwinds are real. But they can vary when you get down to the market and property level. “At some point, the headwinds will abate,” Chang commented. “As that happens, core commercial real estate drivers like demographics, slowing construction, and pent-up demand will reassert." Read the report for the full details and context. DOWNLOAD THE Q3 2026 REPORT Key Takeaways Economic conditions in the Portland region moderated during the third quarter of 2026. Overall vacancy rose to 23.9%, while quarterly net absorption was minimally negative at 21,000 sf, bringing YTD absorption to negative 627,000 sf. Despite ongoing occupancy hurdles, leasing activity remained relatively active with nearly 1.4 msf transacted YTD. New construction remains effectively absent, with no office space currently under construction, limiting future supply additions and allowing market fundamentals to gradually stabilize as vacant space is naturally absorbed over time. Average full-service asking rents dropped 3.8% YOY to $32.54 psf, as property owners continued prioritizing occupancy within a highly competitive leasing environment. Economy: Labor Market Moderates Economic conditions in the Portland region moderated during the third quarter of 2026. Total nonfarm employment declined 1.7% to just over 1.2 million jobs, while the Portland unemployment held steady year-over-year – at 5.0%, it remained 80 basis points higher than the national rate of 4.2%. Looking ahead, while employment growth is expected to remain muted, relatively stable labor market conditions should support a gradual recovery in office leasing activity as occupiers gain greater confidence in long-term space planning. Supply and Demand: Market Continues to Rebalance The Portland office market continued to navigate challenging demand conditions during the third quarter, as occupiers remained selective and continued to prioritize efficiency in their space requirements. Overall vacancy rose to 23.9%, while quarterly net absorption was minimally negative at 21,000 square feet (sf), bringing year-to-date absorption to negative 627,000 sf. Despite ongoing occupancy hurdles, leasing activity remained relatively active with nearly 1.4 million square feet transacted year-to-date. New construction remains effectively absent, with no office space currently under construction, limiting future supply additions and allowing market fundamentals to gradually stabilize as vacant space is naturally absorbed over time. Pricing: Focus on Concession Packages Average full-service asking rents dropped 3.8% YOY to $32.54 per square foot (psf), as property owners continued prioritizing occupancy within a highly competitive leasing environment. Rather than significantly reducing quoted rents, many landlords have focused on concession packages including tenant improvement allowances, free rent and flexible lease structures to attract tenants. Premium Class A properties continue to outperform the broader market, with average Class A asking rents reaching $36.80 psf, reflecting ongoing tenant preference for well-located, amenity-rich buildings that support evolving workplace strategies. items.title: U.S. Retail Demand Remains Solid as Limited Construction Keeps Space Tight
items.description: U.S. Retail Demand Remains Solid as Limited Construction Keeps Space Tight Phoebe Schmidt • 10/29/2026 Q3 U.S. Retail Marketbeat Shopping centers recorded 3.5 million square feet of net absorption in Q3, with fitness, wellness and value retailers leading leasing activity New York -- U.S. shopping center demand remained solid in the third quarter of 2026 as retailers backfilled vacated stores and selectively expanded their footprints, according to Cushman & Wakefield's latest U.S. Retail MarketBeat report . Limited construction continued to support market fundamentals, with national vacancy holding steady at 5.9%, well below the historical average of 7.4%. Net absorption totaled 3.5 million square feet in Q3, the second-strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2023, bringing year-to-date absorption into positive territory at 1.2 million square feet. The improvement followed first-half declines that reflected seasonal weakness and the effects of store closures in 2025. "Retail demand has remained solid beneath the quarterly fluctuations," said James Bohnaker , Principal Economist at Cushman & Wakefield. "Retailers are backfilling space left by earlier closures and continuing to expand selectively. For tenants looking to grow, finding the right space in a quality shopping center remains a challenge." Fitness, wellness and value-oriented retailers are leading categories for leasing activity, reflecting a continued shift toward consumer services and demand for affordable shopping options. Discount retailers accounted for 1,046 store openings year to date, while off-price apparel retailers added 214 locations. New construction remained limited, with just 2.3 million square feet delivered during the quarter. The development pipeline represented only 0.4% of existing inventory. National asking rents reached $25.80 per square foot, up 2.2% year over year, although the pace of growth moderated. "With so little new space being built, even modest expansion can keep availability tight," Bohnaker said. "Consumer spending is holding steady, but retailers remain disciplined about where they open stores. Well-located centers with strong tenant mixes are best positioned to capture that demand." Demand was positive across several regions. The West absorbed 1.4 million square feet and remained the only region to record positive absorption in every quarter of 2026, led in Q3 by Phoenix, the Inland Empire and Orange County. The Northeast recorded 1.2 million square feet of absorption, with vacancy declining in eight of its 11 tracked markets. The Midwest led regional asking rent growth at 3.6% year over year, with Columbus, Cincinnati and St. Louis among the strongest-performing markets nationally. The South accounted for 52% of year-to-date construction completions but maintained the lowest regional vacancy rate at 5.7%. Cushman & Wakefield expects retail fundamentals to remain resilient through year-end, supported by limited new supply and continued tenant demand. Performance will vary by market and property, with location, tenant quality and retailers' value propositions remaining key differentiators. items.description: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Housing Market Ranking By Hannah Jones Oct 29, 2026 Introduction The summer housing market lacked its usual energy as volatile, generally rising mortgage rates eroded affordability and buyer confidence. Early-year affordability wins gave way to higher housing costs. By the best time to buy , mortgage rates were above 7% , and buyers had to confront challenging financing headwinds even as broader market conditions, including more inventory and signs of seller flexibility , lined up in their favor. The 30-year fixed rate now averages 7.40%, up from 6.27% a year ago. On the same loan, today’s higher rate adds roughly 12% to the, in many cases, already-high monthly payment, enough to put some buyers’ plans on hold. The national picture masks a sharper regional divide . The Northeast and Midwest continue to see relatively strong demand and limited supply, which keeps sellers in the driver’s seat. The South and West are more balanced, with both buyers and sellers having room to negotiate. There is some good news for buyers. Inventory has grown in much of the country, price reductions are more common and asking prices have even softened in many markets. Buyers who can handle higher rates have more room to offset them with a lower price or seller concessions. They can also beat the headline rate by shopping lenders, improving their credit score and making a larger down payment. Planning for rate volatility and building flexibility into their housing budget can help them succeed even in a difficult market. This challenging backdrop gives some context as to why this quarter’s ranking elevates markets where a dollar goes farther. Nineteen of the top 20 markets are in the Midwest and Northeast where, in many cases, prices still pencil out against local incomes. The Fall 2026 WSJ/Realtor.com Housing Market Ranking highlights the markets best positioned to deliver stability, livability and long-term value. Sellers responded by pricing lower and reducing prices more, but transaction volume still suffered. In this challenging affordability environment, metros that combine lower prices with steady demand, improving supply conditions, and strong quality-of-life fundamentals continue to stand out. items.title: U.S. Economy Accelerated in the Third Quarter of 2026
items.description: U.S. Economy Accelerated in the Third Quarter of 2026 October 29, 2026 Jing Fu No Comments The U.S. economy grew at a faster pace in the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger consumer spending, robust business investment, and increased government spending. However, residential investment remained a weak spot, highlighting the continued challenges facing the housing sector amid elevated borrowing costs. According to the “advance” estimate released by the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), real gross domestic product (GDP) expanded at an annual rate of 3.4% in the third quarter, up from a 2.2% increase in the second quarter of 2026. The acceleration suggests that overall economic activity strengthened during the summer, although the advance estimate remains subject to revision. The latest GDP report also showed that inflationary pressures eased in the third quarter. The price index for gross domestic purchases rose 3.0% in the third quarter, down from 5.6% in the second quarter. The Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, which measures inflation (or deflation) across various consumer expenses and reflects changes in consumer behavior, increased 2.1%, compared with a 5.0% increase in the previous quarter. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE price index increased 2.5%, easing from 3.3% in the second quarter. Breaking down the third-quarter data further, growth in real GDP primarily reflected gains in consumer spending, investment, and government spending, which were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased during the quarter. Consumer spending, the backbone of the U.S. economy, increased at an annual rate of 3.8% in the third quarter, following a similar pace of growth in the second quarter. The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods. Gross private domestic investment continued to support economic growth in the third quarter, particularly through strong business investment in equipment and intellectual property products. Investment associated with artificial intelligence and information-processing equipment contributed to the expansion, while residential investment remained weak. Nonresidential fixed investment increased 12.7% in the third quarter. Strong gains in equipment (+20.9%) and intellectual property products (+8.8%) supported business investment. Meanwhile, residential fixed investment (RFI) declined 3.3%. Within the residential category, investment in single-family permanent site structures decreased 5.0% at an annual rate, multifamily permanent site structures rose 0.3%, and spending on improvements rose 2.7%. Government spending increased 5.3% in the third quarter, contributing to the acceleration in overall economic growth. Trade activity was a drag on GDP growth in the third quarter. Exports declined, while imports increased. Because imports are subtracted from GDP, the increase in imports further weighed on headline growth, partly offsetting the positive contributions from consumer spending, investment, and government spending. items.title: The housing market gets a positive Fed day for a change
items.description: On Wednesday we got an October surprise: the Fed day was eerily calm, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh looking comfortable on stage and offering a slightly dovish take on the future — if a few things improve. I believe the Fed wants to take back all the interest rate cuts from last year, and then they can assess what is happening in the economy. Of course, the Iran conflict and Trade War 2.0 have complicated their job, but today, given that markets were at one point pricing in five to six rate hikes, was a positive day. Last I checked, the 10-year was at 5.02%, down after Google reported a bad quarter. The Fed's press statement was short and simple, but two things caught my attention. 1. The economy is strong vs. solid First, the Fed chose to use the word "strong" instead of "solid" on purpose to signal it won’t cut rates and will continue reversing last year's interest rate cuts while inflation stays above target. “ Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Warsh said jobless claims data remain low and that the Fed fully intends to bring inflation back to the 2% target, no compromise. He also said the Fed will hold one fewer voting meeting in 2027 and two fewer meetings in 2028; this approach might leave the Fed open to more 50-basis-point cuts or hikes. However, that is another story for another time. 2. Warsh liked the market drama against AI I got a strong sense that Warsh liked the market getting more restrictive and that we even saw some AI companies shed some blood recently. My theme in the HousingWire Daily podcast lately borrows from The Predator movie: the AI god king can bleed — and that it means you can kill it. I think Warsh was implying no company is invincible, and that if the market gets more restrictive, things can change, as they recently did. He also talked about how the 10-year yield rolled over even though oil prices have been elevated this month. I believe the 10-year yield rollover is more market-driven, as the 10-year was pricing in more rate hikes than the Fed was targeting at the time. The term premium on the 10-year yield was elevated as it headed to the October high. If the 10-year had closed over the key level of 5.35%, bond yields had the potential to rise much higher, faster, as the markets would be pricing in a much more aggressive Fed rate hike cycle, but, smartly, they chose not to go that route. Warsh seems to enjoy that everyone is taking the Fed seriously and that the markets have already done a lot of the work for them. This reaffirms my assumption that all they want to do is take back the rate cuts from last year and then reassess what is going on. One side note was that Fed Governor Lisa Cook — who is usually a dove — voted to raise rates, which I 100% believe was a trolling tactic on her part since Trump still wants to fire her . All in all, it wasn’t a bad day; the 10-year yield is above 5% still today, but considering the market was trying to price in five to six rate hikes, and there hasn’t been any end to the conflict or the trade war, I consider this a victory for the month of October. For housing, the worst-case scenario has been averted and we bought some time, giving space for the conflict to end and the trade war to cool off a bit. What I am hoping for is that we get some more clarity on both of those two items, and then the Fed can make the rate hike cycle just a few rate hikes, and then we'll take it from there. items.title: Why Howard Hanna was missing from Open Real Estate launch list
items.description: When the Open Real Estate initiative launched on Monday, one brokerage’s name was noticeably missing from the list of founding firms and initial participants. “It would have been nice to be at the table, but obviously those guys didn’t see me at their level,” Hoby Hanna, the CEO of Howard Hanna Real Estate Services , told HousingWire . Since the nationwide residential real estate data sharing initiative was announced on Monday, Hanna, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said the Open Real Estate founders have been in touch with him to discuss the initiative. “We were approached to see if we’d like to have a discussion to learn more and find out what direction they want to go in,” Hanna said. “I’ve agreed to meet with them, but no dates or anything have been set yet. I’m curious to learn more because right now I can only speculate off off the information that is publicly available.” Hanna said he is really curious to learn what the end goal of the initiative is and if they have any plans in place for governance and funding. As of right now, given the limited amount of information he has, Hanna said he is unsure if Howard Hanna, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, will join Open Real Estate. “We have invested a lot of time and money into the platform we have built, HannaList ,” Hanna said. “We are moving forward with that and we’ve cooperated with MLSs to build it, so I’d really have to understand what the end game is and get a sense of if they can really pull it off before deciding if we will participate.” Hanna noted that he was previously part of the disbanded Project Upstream , which in some ways may add to his skepticism of this initiative actually getting off the ground. “One of the challenges with Project Upstream, beyond maybe the technology available at the time not being what we needed, was that there were too many people involved,” Hanna said. “Just so many proverbial cooks in the kitchen with too many disparate interests from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), to the MLS, to brokerages, agents and the consumers.” Although disappointed to not have been included in the initial conversations, Hanna said he is glad to see some of the industry’s largest players coming together. “One of the industry’s other problems in the past has been that not everybody is willing to talk and [there is] this lack of trust,” Hanna. “Sure, I would have loved to have been at the table since it is something that we as a company have been innovating on and growing already and could give the pros and cons on. I think there needs to be reform in our industry, and I do think that the large brokerage firms need to be the ones driving it because they have so many people they impact.” For its part, a spokesperson for Open Real Estate told HousingWire that the initiative was “founded on the belief that the future of housing information should be shaped by the entire industry.” “We welcome the perspectives of all industry leaders, and our announcement was just the beginning of this collaborative effort,” the spokesperson added. “We have already received significant interest from the sector since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers.” Related More: Clear Cooperation Hoby Hanna Howard Hanna Real Estate Services

items.title: MLS executives weigh Open Real Estate and listing control
items.description: The announcement of the Open Real Estate initiative caused quite a stir this week , as industry professionals and analysts ponder how the national residential real estate data-sharing initiative will fit into the real estate ecosystem and what impact it will have. On the surface, the initiative, which is focused on fostering agent and broker cooperation through the sharing of residential real estate listings and includes a rule that requires members to submit a property to the Open Real Estate database within one business day of signing a listing agreement with a homeowner, may sound a lot like the MLS. But, the leaders of the initiatives’ four founding brokerage firms, AGNT , (the parent company of eXp Realty and NextHome franchises), HomeServices of America , Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group , all RealTrends Verified brokerages, have said that Open Real Estate is not a national MLS and is in no way replacing local MLSs. According to initial announcements regarding Open Real Estate, listings input into its database will then be pushed out to the MLS and other portals and sites, or the listing can be directly entered into a brokerage’s local MLS, which will then supply the listing to portals, other sites and Open Real Estate. The founders have also stressed that they will leave rulemaking and enforcement up to the local associations and MLSs. MLS impact Despite these assurances, some in the industry still believe this could lead to the demise of MLSs as they currently exist, but MLS leaders aren’t so sure. “My perspective is that Open Real Estate is a positive development for the industry and an opportunity to rethink how brokers and MLSs work together to support the businesses and consumers they serve,” Tim Dain, the CEO of Northstar MLS , told HousingWire . “I’m encouraged to see major brokerages taking a more active role in shaping the infrastructure that supports their businesses and the consumers they serve.” Dain, a 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner, added that he doesn’t see Open Real Estate as “inherently threatening to MLSs,” but rather as a “significant opportunity” for brokers and MLSs to work together to modernize infrastructure, eliminate unnecessary duplication, improve data quality and create a more efficient marketplace. Brian Donnellan, the CEO and president of Bright MLS has a similar view. “I can certainly see how people can say that this is the end of the MLS, but don’t I see it that way,” Donnellan, a 2025 and 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said. “When I look at all they want to accomplish, I think it verifies that we at Bright have been doing things right for a while.” In September 2025 , Bright MLS announced the launch of a joint venture with multi-MLS listing management platform Ocusell to co-develop and license technology solutions and services for brokers, agents and MLSs nationwide. Ocusell’s technology has since been used to help independent brokerage Howard Hanna Real Estate Services launch HannaList , an internal listing portal designed to give sellers an early-access marketing option before a listing is widely distributed and to give agents a single point of listing entry. Position of control For Saul Klein, the CEO of San Diego MLS (SDMLS), this is exactly what Open Real Estate is about: first point of entry. “Today, the MLS is still the first point of entry and there have been attempts over the years to change this, but nobody has been successful,” Klein said. According to Klein, whoever is the first point of entry is the one in the “position of control,” and with that position comes responsibilities like governance, something Open Real Estate’s founders have said their organization is not interested in. Due to this, he sees a world where Open Real Estate could be a threat to MLSs, but he says that it's still too early to tell. “It is still a pipe dream,” Klein said. “They have to build the technology and integrate each company’s technology and workflows, and they are clear on MLS policies with their own 24-hour rule, but it is still too early to tell and MLSs can change their value proposition as this evolves.” Donnellan says that Open Real Estate is just an example of brokerages deciding to take things into their own hands after the industry was too slow to react. “These brokers have real problems that haven’t been solved yet,” he said. “This is an opportunity for everybody and if it creates more competition in the MLS space, that is good. It will bring out the best in everybody.” Open Real Estate and the MLS However, Donnellan said that this may create some winners and losers in the MLS space, leading to negative outcomes for MLSs that are unable or unwilling to compete or adapt. “It's probably a good thing that brokers get to choose who it is that they want to work with and how they work, and it's probably better that the brokers get to set more guidelines,” Donnellan said. As for how Open Real Estate will work alongside MLSs, MLS leaders are generally optimistic. At Bright MLS, Donnellan is confident that his MLS will be able to collaborate with Open Real Estate. “I think Open Real Estate’s goals are something Bright has been working towards for a long time — effectively working across the country, reducing some of the obsolete, outdated and redundant technology,” Donnellan said. “We’ve always been there to work for our brokers, and we’ve always wanted to work with other MLSs. Now, with the tide is going out, we are going to see who actually does want to work with brokers and other MLSs and who doesn't want to work. You're not going to be able to run and hide now.” Klein, however, still has questions, including if they can convince agents to adopt a new work flow and how the entity will eventually support itself if it does not have a complete data set. “The portals have made billions of dollars in revenue from leads, which shows that MLS data is worth something, but only when aggregated as a full data set,” Klein said. items.title: Blackstone Mortgage Trust Reports Unexpected Q3 Net Loss
items.description: Blackstone Mortgage Trust reported a $327M net loss for the third quarter, news that sent stocks tumbling. Unsplash/Clarisse Croset Shares were at $9.95 during premarket trading on Thursday. Though they had rebounded during trading hours to just under $11 per share, they were still down 11% over the last month and down roughly 42% over the last six months. As of about 3 p.m. ET Thursday, BXMT shares were trading up 3.75%, or $10.94 per share. Leadership pointed to higher interest rates and challenges facing the office market. "While higher rates and an elongated office recovery impacted our reserves and book value, our watchlist is now at the lowest level since 2019, and the remainder of our legacy portfolio is performing well and shrinking rapidly," Blackstone Mortgage Trust CEO Tim Johnson said in a statement. The company impaired roughly $800M of loans on its books, the vast majority being office assets, indicating that it still has work to do balancing its portfolio, Johnson said on an earnings call Thursday. Leadership said it is still on track to meet or exceed its previously announced goal of reducing office and legacy loans by 40% by year-end. Johnson said higher interest rates will have the greatest impact on some of the REIT's pre-2023 investments, which is why it's prioritizing the sale of older loans. Blackstone Mortgage Trust's total net revenue rose to $141.9M from $132.6M in the same period in 2025 , but interest and related income fell to $280.6M from approximately $346M a year ago, below the Visible Alpha consensus of $293.5M, according to Seeking Alpha . items.title: Philly Hospitals Seek Cost Savings From Architects, Builders
items.description: Hospitals across greater Philadelphia face a challenging operating environment, and with federal support expected to dry up, executives are looking to the ancillary businesses they work with for help. Pexels/K Architecture and construction firms that depend on these projects can do more to help keep capital budgets in check as healthcare systems respond to sustained patient demand, CEOs from across the region said Tuesday at Bisnow ’s Pennsylvania Healthcare Real Estate Summit, held at the Crystal Tea Room in Philadelphia. “You’ve got to help us in our ecosystem,” University of Pennsylvania Health System CEO Kevin Mahoney said. “Get on our team. We’re getting paid less.” The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia is spending nearly $2.6B to build a new patient tower in West Philadelphia, CEO Joseph Mitchell said. The 20-story building is due in 2028. While he is proud of the project, Mitchell said the institution can’t afford to keep spending like this in the current climate. “That’s just unaffordable in the long term,” he said. “Partner with your clients to find ways to reduce these costs. It’s a two-way street.” Hospitals' already strained operating margins are facing more issues from federal spending cuts that lead to an increase in uncompensated care. Last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a $1T cut to Medicaid through 2034, which is expected to cause more than 10 million Americans to lose their health insurance coverage over that period. This is a particularly grave issue for cash-strapped rural hospitals. More than 100 have shuttered over the past decade, and another 700 are at risk of closing, according to a July report from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform. Hospitals face additional economic challenges when looking to build new facilities. Construction costs across Eastern Pennsylvania were up 2.2% month-over-month and 11.2% year-over-year in September, according to a report from the local branch of Associated Builders and Contractors. Mitchell acknowledged that construction costs are ballooning across the U.S. and that health systems sometimes don’t pick the cheapest ways to do projects. For example, CHOP has opted to utilize union labor on the tower. Last-minute changes to hospital projects that are commonplace in the industry also add extra costs, Mitchell said. But ultimately, the executive said something has to break: “Can we find ways to limit astronomical growth in capital spending?” Bisnow/Noah Zucker LF Driscoll's Mike Dikon, Thomas Jefferson University's Joseph Cacchione, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia's Joseph Mitchell, Tower Health's Michael Stern, Highmark Health's Karen Hanlon, Geisinger's Terry Gilliland, Cooper University Health Care's Anthony Mazzarelli and University of Pennsylvania Health System's Kevin Mahoney Mahoney suggested that less traditional construction techniques could be part of the solution. He said Penn Medicine’s 17-story, 504-bed Pavilion came online in West Philly in 2021 after the system spent $1.6B. The project was 30% modular, Mahoney said. He thought projects should be closer to 70% prefabricated as a way to rein in construction budgets. Penn Medicine signed a 40K SF lease for its first Delaware location in February. The space in suburban Wilmington will be focused on primary care and some specialty services. Artificial intelligence is just as hot a topic in the design and building world as anywhere else, but Cooper University Health Care CEO Anthony Mazzarelli said healthcare systems aren't seeing the technology create shorter construction timelines or anything else that would save them money. “That's how long that took two years ago. You just told me you're using all this AI stuff. How are you passing on that efficiency to us?” he said. “We're the one throat to choke from the government when it comes to spending, but it's also going to hurt everybody else.” Earlier at Tuesday's event, a different panel was asked about unconventional techniques that could be used to expedite projects. CHOP Assistant Vice President of Facilities Project Management and Construction Brian Gardner floated organizationwide standardized construction plans. While designing and coming to a consensus on those plans can be an arduous process, he said the work pays off down the line and is one of the few meaningful levers healthcare systems can pull to shorten construction timelines. "Standardization is probably one of the low-hanging fruits that organizations can work through because decisions come quicker,” Gardner said. The CEOs’ pleas for cost savings come as regional hospital system players expect higher construction prices in Pennsylvania amid the data center boom. Many of the contractors and suppliers that hospital systems depend on have been focused on getting a piece of the artificial intelligence data center boom, a trend that is already making it harder to build healthcare projects in other markets, like Houston . “We’re already seeing it with the data centers, believe it or not,” Guthrie Senior Vice President Joseph Sawyer said. He recalled being given a yearlong lead time for critical components such as generators and air handlers. Increased competition for construction workers is also straining construction budgets. “How do we address, when we’re trying to do pro formas nationally, the impact of 50% labor increases because we can’t find enough qualified labor?” Limbach Vice President Jay Levin said. KQT Health owner Todd Strine said he believes there is no end in sight and that it would behoove health systems to expedite their construction decision-making. “Prices are going to go way up,” he said. “If you’re going to make a large decision, I think it’s better to do it sooner than later.” See more photos from Tuesday's event below.
