Processing Content Investors' concerns over whether artificial intelligence companies will be able to handle their debt loads helped to push the 10-year Treasury yield back under the 5% floor this past week. This reduction helped the average for the 30-year fixed rate mortgage fall by 8 basis points for a second consecutive week , Freddie Mac said. But the 10-year Treasury still remains close to 5%, making mortgage industry observers wary about its effect on long-term rates, even with the Federal Open Market Committee's decision to stand pat on Wednesday. "We often see more movement from mortgage rates in anticipation of Federal Reserve meetings than we do once the decisions are actually announced, and with this widely expected pause we didn't even see that," said Kate Wood, NerdWallet's lending expert. "It's been a while since the Fed was the main character in the mortgage rates narrative." If anything, it is the market reaction to what is happening with the AI companies, putting money into Treasurys even with higher inflation, that has been driving mortgage rates lower, Wood said. Mortgage rates this week The 30-year FRM averaged 7.24% for Oct. 29, the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey reported. This is down from last week's 7.32%. However, a year ago, this product averaged 6.17% or 108 basis points lower than the current rate. For this week, the 15-year FRM averaged 6.6%, also a decline of 8 basis points from the Oct. 22 PMMS. For the same week in 2025 it averaged 5.41%. "The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers," said Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist, in a press release. Lender Price data posted on the National Mortgage News website on Thursday morning had the 30-year FRM at 7.55%, more than 20 basis points lower than a week ago, reflecting the changed Treasury environment. The 10-year was 4.98% as of 11 a.m. Last Thursday, the 10-year closed at 4.95% after ending the previous day at 5.15%. Still, most observers are holding to their views for rates to stay above 7% for at least the next two months, if not beyond. How originators viewed the FOMC announcement "Higher for longer isn't a forecast anymore, it's the environment," said Hector Amendola, the president of SimplyPMG. "I don't know where rates go and I won't pretend to." The supply of homes for sale is better now than a year ago and based on what he is seeing in his own pipeline, sellers are more willing to make concessions. "Buyers doing well right now stopped watching the announcement and started working on the long game and focusing on what they qualify for today," Amendola said. In a statement issued after the Fed decision but before this morning's Personal Consumption Expenditures index release , Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage said the FOMC is "very likely" to hike at its December meeting if inflation hasn't improved. "We can hope that the markets remain stable and last week's rate improvements hold," Cohn continued. "Where mortgage rates go next will largely depend on oil prices and the war in Iran." In the opinion of mortgage and structured credit investment strategy company Dundon E1, the most important development for mortgage rates is the guidance the FOMC issued with the decision, said Victor Baev, its chief investment officer, on Wednesday. "Two members of the committee voted in favor of another increase, and the statement kept the possibility of a further hike at the December meeting on the table," Baev said. "That tells the bond market that short-term rates are likely to remain at or above current levels for an extended period." This likelihood is already priced into the 10-year, one of the mechanisms used to set mortgage rates, he said. Mostly agreeing with Cohn, Baev said inflation is what home buyers have to look at, not what the Fed does at any individual meeting. "The 30-year fixed rate has risen roughly 70 basis points since late August as the market adjusted to the September increase, and last week's reading represented the first weekly decline in two months," Baev noted. items.title: Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar
items.description: Fannie Mae Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 28, 2026, 5:29 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Why Fannie Mae came out ahead in earnings despite mixed impacts from higher rates, and has new reason to press forward with title alternatives. Supporting Data: Fannie found borrowers' collective savings from appraisal and title alternatives so far this year have been over $100 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Fannie Mae reported its highest net revenues since 2023 and revealed significant mission-related borrower savings from title and appraisal alternative initiatives in the third quarter, when it contended with mixed impacts from higher rates but was still able to hold costs for lenders relatively low. Consumer savings from the title and appraisal waiver programs show these alternatives got enough use to drive a 7-figure reduction in origination expenses. They also reinforce a recent executive order backing both and transitioning Fannie's title alternative pilot to a national program with monitoring. Processing Content "Our efforts to provide appraisal and title insurance alternatives helped borrowers save an estimated $141 million in closing costs so far this year," Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae said during the government-related loan buyer's earnings call. Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae Fannie was able to support such housing affordability initiatives with $4.2 billion in net income, representing a 5% rise from the previous quarter and an 8% increase from a year ago, even though higher rates diminished the industry originations it buys. The government-sponsored enterprise's executives explained why during its earnings call. Why fewer acquisitions didn't hurt revenue "Changes in interest rates affect various aspects of our financial results. For example, in single-family, while higher rates tend to reduce acquisition volumes, they also slow prepayments and book runoff, helping to preserve guaranty revenues," Chief Financial Officer Chryssa Halley noted during the company's call. Fannie's core guaranty business fueled 79% of its $7.7 billion in total net revenues, which drove the government-sponsored enterprise's earnings gain. Single-family loan acquisition volumes did fall by roughly 21% from the previous quarter and around 11% from a year earlier to $88 billion in line with some industry declines, but with refinancing representing only $18 billion of that total, prepayments for Fannie were reduced. Refi activity in the dominant single-family business matched year-ago levels but was down nearly 53% from the previous quarter. In addition to affecting prepayments and loan volume in the quarter, this may have another impact, according to Halley. "From an allowance perspective, slow prepayments extend the expected life of our loans, which combined with higher mortgage costs for certain borrowers can increase our expected credit losses," she said. Serious and 60-day delinquencies in the single-family sector remained historically low but have been drifting generally higher in the past year, ending at 62 and 92 basis points, respectively, in the third quarter. They were both nearly 20 basis points lower than a year earlier. Sixty-day delinquencies were 7 basis points lower the previous quarter. Serious delinquencies were 4 basis points lower compared to the same period. Thirty-day delinquencies matched the previous quarter's 1.09%, but were below the 1% level reported a year earlier. Fannie recorded a total single- and multifamily allowance for credit losses of $1.1 billion, offset by other developments that included $630 million in fair value gains. The GSE also reported $94 million in investment gains. It additionally took $1 billion in net unrealized losses in its available-for-sale portfolio. Efficiency initiatives and regulatory capital Fannie also engaged in further efficiency initiatives during the quarter that Halley said offset some personnel costs for increased salaries, benefits and a $28 million severance expense. Expenditures on occupancy and technology were $52 million lower than the previous quarter. Fannie reported a total adjusted capital deficit of $11 billion for the quarter, down from $14 billion in the previous three-month period. Its illustrative return on average required tier 1 capital was 11.1% in the quarter, up from 10.8%. "Despite volatility across aspects of our financial results, we increased net income both quarter over quarter and year over year, growing net worth to more than $119 billion while reducing our regulatory capital deficit," Halley said. items.description: Partners Development Breaks Ground on 80,000 SF Industrial Project in Seguin, Texas by Taylor Williams October 29, 2026 October 29, 2026 3 SEGUIN, TEXAS — Partners Development, an affiliate of Partners Real Estate, has broken ground on an 80,000-square-foot industrial project in Seguin, located northeast of San Antonio. The project, which will feature two 40,000-square-foot buildings, represents Phase I of Seguin Commerce Park, a development that is ultimately planned to comprise eight buildings totaling 234,600 square feet. Palladius Capital Management provided construction financing for Phase I of the project, which is slated for a late spring/early summer 2027 delivery. Partners is also marketing the buildings for lease and/or sale. Savills arranged Year Up United’s approximately 33,700-square-foot Boston lease and provided project management services to prepare the headquarters for occupancy. Managing director Brett Tynes worked alongside senior managing director Matt Perry in Boston and corporate managing directors Brandon Nasatir in Chicago and Steve Woodworth in Providence. Zac Sargent of Savills Program and Project Management spearheaded the project management services for the Boston transaction. The Boston move is part of Year Up United’s evolving national footprint. The organization recently signed an approximately 12,600-square-foot lease in Providence and a nearly 13,000-square-foot lease in Chicago’s Two Prudential Plaza, both scheduled to open by the end of this year. items.title: Chicago/Midwest People & Company News, week of October 30, 2026
items.description: Chicago/Midwest People & Company News, week of October 30, 2026 Colliers announced that Jeff Winters has been appointed managing director and brokerage market leader for Kansas City. In his new role, Winters will oversee all brokerage operations, including recruitment, retention, and business development for the market. He will report to Jeremy Jacobs, President | Central Region Brokerage. Winters succeeds Ed Elder, who has led the Kansas City office for the past 10 years. Elder will remain with Colliers as a Principal, focusing on client relationships, strategic pursuits, and new business development. Farbman Group announced the hiring of two team members and one promotion across its family of companies. Tom Spirl joined Farbman Group, Chris Huston joined Huntington Maintenance and Liam Longe received a promotion. Spirl has joined as an engineer, bringing over 20 years of hands-on experience in facility maintenance and operations. Huston is joining Huntington Maintenance as a maintenance technician, bringing 11 years of experience in property maintenance across residential, office and retail properties. After excelling as a property management intern for over two years at Farbman Group, Longe has been promoted to assistant property manager. Related Midwest , in partnership with 210 Design House , recently hosted its 23 rd annual Charity Golf Classic at Chicago’s Harborside International Golf Course. The event attracted 300 real estate and construction industry professionals, with more than 70 participating foursomes, raising over $500,000 for three Chicago-area nonprofits. Throughout its 23-year history, the Golf Classic has raised nearly $9 million to support organizations that provide services and programs for children and youth across Chicago. Greenstone Partners' Senior Director Michael Duckler represented the purchaser in the $13.6 million sale of Heritage Manor Apartments, an 84-unit multifamily portfolio in Orland Park, Illinois. The portfolio comprises seven 12-unit buildings in Chicago’s southwest suburban market. SpringView Investments secured the portfolio with plans to invest approximately $2.5 million in apartment upgrades. With experience in marketing and communications for academic nonprofits and corporate clients, including Hearst Media, Hilton, and Coldwell Banker, Kilman has written about commercial real estate, environmental, social, and corporate governance (ESG), technology, healthcare, and philanthropy. She was born and raised in California and graduated with a degree in public relations. In her spare time, Kilman enjoys hiking and traveling to new locations with her family.
